overview:
“Sakal-arhat praise” refers to the Sakalārhat Stotra (सकलाऽर्हत्स्तोत्रम्), a celebrated Jain hymn in Sanskrit that offers comprehensive praise to all Arhats, specifically the twenty-four Tīrthaṅkaras. The term “sakal-arhat” literally means “all Arhats,” and the stotra is structured as a mangalācaraṇa—an auspicious invocation—meditating on Arhatship itself as the foundation of liberation and then individually extolling each Tīrthaṅkara’s qualities, virtues, and spiritual functions.

Historically, the Sakalārhat Stotra is attributed primarily to the twelfth‑century Śvetāmbara polymath Hemacandrācārya (often titled Kalikālasarvajña, “omniscient of the Kali age”). He composed it at the beginning of his epic Triṣaṣṭiśalākāpuruṣacaritra (“Lives of the Sixty‑three Illustrious Persons”) as the opening praise to the Arhats and as a doctrinal and devotional frame for the narratives that follow. Because of its poetic beauty and doctrinal density, the hymn was later transmitted as an independent liturgical text and incorporated into ritual cycles such as pakṣik, caumāsik, and samvatsarī pratikramaṇa among Śvetāmbara Mūrtipūjaka communities.

The stotra begins with universal praise of Arhatship: Arhathood is described as the “foundation of all Arhats,” the “abode of the Śrī of emancipation,” and the “light of the three worlds.” It emphasizes that the Arhats purify beings in all realms through their name, image, substance, and actual presence. Subsequent verses then praise each of the twenty‑four Tīrthaṅkaras in sequence, starting with Ṛṣabha (Ādinātha) and continuing through Mahāvīra. Each verse uses rich metaphor—sun, moon, clouds, kalpa‑tree, physician, ocean of compassion—to highlight specific doctrinal themes: omniscience (kevalajñāna), non‑one‑sidedness (anekāntavāda), the nectar of syādvāda, the fourfold dharma, and the universal benefit of Tīrthaṅkara‑karma.

In liturgical practice, Sakalārhat praise functions on several levels. Devotionally, it cultivates reverence and gratitude toward the Tīrthaṅkaras as perfected beings who have shown the path to liberation. Doctrinally, it compresses key Jain philosophical ideas—karma theory, omniscience, non‑violence, non‑possessiveness, and the multi‑faceted nature of truth—into poetic images that can be memorized and recited. Ritually, its recitation at the start of major confession and reflection rites (pratikramaṇa) frames the practitioner’s ethical self‑examination within the horizon of Arhat ideals, reminding laypeople and ascetics alike that the ultimate goal is the realization of Arhatship.

From a textual and historical perspective, Sakalārhat praise also illustrates how Jain communities have used stotra literature to bridge scriptural study and lived practice. Commentaries by later ācāryas and gaṇis dissect the compound words, grammar, and imagery of the verses, making the hymn a pedagogical tool for learning Sanskrit and Jain doctrine. At the same time, the hymn’s status as a revered prayer means that it is accessible to non‑specialists, often recited in temples and homes. Thus, “Sakal-arhat praise” is not only a specific hymn but also a paradigm of Jain devotional and doctrinal engagement with the Arhat ideal: a sustained, poetic meditation on the qualities of liberated beings that guides the practitioner toward ethical refinement and spiritual aspiration.

Modern scholarship and community education materials treat the Sakalārhat Stotra as a key example of medieval Jain Sanskrit hymnody. They note Hemacandra’s role in systematizing Jain narrative and philosophical traditions and highlight how the hymn’s metaphors encode complex doctrinal positions in aesthetically compelling language. At the same time, traditional commentaries stress that the ultimate purpose of Sakal-arhat praise is not mere literary appreciation but transformation of the reciter’s inner disposition—cultivating humility, non‑attachment, and a desire to emulate, in however limited a way, the virtues of the Arhats.

primary_sources.title: Sakalārhat Stotra (सकलाऽर्हत्स्तोत्रम्), opening verses
primary_sources.author: Hemacandrācārya (primary verses), with later additions by subsequent ācāryas
primary_sources.original_text:
सकलाऽऽर्हत्–प्रतिष्ठानमधिष्ठानं शिवश्रियः ।
भूर्भुवःस्वस्त्रयीशानमार्हन्त्यं प्रणिदध्महे ॥१॥

नामाऽऽकृतिद्रव्यभावैः पुनतस्त्रिजगज्जनम् ।
क्षेत्रे काले च सर्वस्मिन्नर्हतः समुपास्महे ॥२॥

आदिमं पृथिवीनाथमादिमं निष्परिग्रहम् ।
आदिमं तीर्थनाथं च ऋषभस्वामिनं स्तुमः ॥३॥
primary_sources.transliteration:
sakalārhat–pratiṣṭhānamadhiṣṭhānaṃ śiva–śriyaḥ |
bhūr–bhuvaḥ–svas–trayīśānam ārhantyaṃ praṇidadhmahe ||1||

nāmā–ākṛti–dravya–bhāvaiḥ punatas–trijagajjanam |
kṣetre kāle ca sarvasminn arhataḥ samupāsmahe ||2||

ādimaṃ pṛthivīnātham ādimaṃ niṣparigraham |
ādimaṃ tīrthanāthaṃ ca ṛṣabhasvāminaṃ stumaḥ ||3||
primary_sources.translation:
1. We meditate on Arhatship, the foundation of all the Arhats, the abode of the auspicious glory of liberation, the light of the three worlds—earth, atmosphere, and heaven.

2. We worship the Arhats, who at all times and in all places purify the beings of the three worlds by their name, their form, their substance, and their actual existence.

3. We praise Lord Ṛṣabha, the first Lord of the earth, the first without possessions, and the first Lord of the tīrtha (spiritual community).
primary_sources.notes: These opening verses establish the core theme of Sakalārhat praise: meditation on Arhatship as such, followed by specific praise of individual Tīrthaṅkaras. The first verse presents Arhatship as the metaphysical foundation and luminous source of emancipation. The second verse introduces a fourfold mode of Arhat presence—name (nāma), image/form (ākṛti), substance (dravya), and actual existence (bhāva)—through which beings are purified across all times and places. The third verse begins the sequential praise of the twenty‑four Tīrthaṅkaras with Ṛṣabha (Ādinātha), emphasizing his status as the first king, first ascetic, and first leader of the Jain community. In Hemacandra’s Triṣaṣṭiśalākāpuruṣacaritra, these verses function as the mangalācaraṇa, framing the entire epic within the horizon of Arhat ideals. Later liturgical usage extracts the hymn as an independent stotra, recited in pratikramaṇa and other devotional contexts.

primary_sources.title: Triṣaṣṭiśalākāpuruṣacaritra, Introduction (English translation)
primary_sources.author: Hemacandrācārya; translated by Helen M. Johnson
primary_sources.original_text:
We meditate on Arhatship, the foundation of all the Arhats, the abode of the Śrī of emancipation, the light of the three worlds—earth, air, and heaven.
We worship the Arhats, who at all times and all places purify the people of the three worlds by their name, representation, substance, and actual existence.
We praise Ṛṣabha Svāmin, who was the first king, the first ascetic, the first head of a congregation.
primary_sources.transliteration: English prose rendering; underlying Sanskrit corresponds to the verses cited above.
primary_sources.translation: This passage is an English prose translation of the opening verses of the Sakalārhat Stotra as embedded in Hemacandra’s Triṣaṣṭiśalākāpuruṣacaritra. It conveys the same doctrinal content: meditation on Arhatship, worship of the Arhats as purifiers of the three worlds, and praise of Ṛṣabha as the first king, ascetic, and leader.
primary_sources.notes: Johnson’s translation, prepared in the early twentieth century, is a key scholarly source for non‑Sanskrit readers. It confirms the placement of Sakalārhat praise at the beginning of Hemacandra’s epic and illustrates how the hymn’s poetic Sanskrit is rendered into accessible English prose. While the translation is interpretive and not a word‑for‑word transliteration, it preserves the central doctrinal motifs and shows how modern scholarship has approached Jain stotra literature.

misconceptions.myth: Sakalārhat praise is only a general, undifferentiated homage and does not address individual Tīrthaṅkaras.
misconceptions.reality: Although the term “sakal-arhat” emphasizes praise of all Arhats collectively, the Sakalārhat Stotra systematically praises each of the twenty‑four Tīrthaṅkaras in sequence. After the initial universal verses on Arhatship, the hymn devotes individual verses to Ṛṣabha, Ajita, Sambhava, Abhinandana, Sumati, Padmaprabha, Supārśva, Candraprabha, Suvidhi, Śītala, Śreyāṃsa, Vāsupūjya, Vimala, Anantajit, Dharmanātha, Śāntinātha, Kunthunātha, Arahanātha, Mallinātha, Munisuvrata, Naminātha, Neminātha, and Mahāvīra, using distinct metaphors and doctrinal emphases for each.

misconceptions.myth: Sakalārhat praise is a purely emotional devotional text with little doctrinal significance.
misconceptions.reality: While the Sakalārhat Stotra is deeply devotional, it is also doctrinally rich. Its verses encode key Jain philosophical concepts—such as anekāntavāda (non‑one‑sidedness), syādvāda (the doctrine of conditioned predication), the nature of Tīrthaṅkara‑karma, omniscience, non‑possessiveness, and the fourfold dharma—through carefully chosen metaphors and technical terms. Traditional commentaries and modern scholarship treat the hymn as a concise doctrinal summary as well as a prayer, and it is used pedagogically to teach both Sanskrit and Jain philosophy.

misconceptions.myth: Sakalārhat praise can be used as a stand‑alone authority for making binding religious rulings or personal life decisions.
misconceptions.reality: The Sakalārhat Stotra is a devotional and doctrinal hymn, not a prescriptive legal or ritual manual. It inspires reverence for the Arhats and summarizes key philosophical ideas, but it does not function as a source of binding rulings on complex issues such as medical decisions, vows involving dependents, or initiation (dīkṣā). For such matters, Jain tradition emphasizes consultation with qualified living teachers (ācāryas, monks, nuns) and, where relevant, professional experts in medicine, mental health, law, or finance. The hymn’s role is to orient the practitioner toward Arhat ideals, not to replace responsible, context‑sensitive guidance.

misconceptions.myth: Only one fixed version of the Sakalārhat Stotra exists, and all communities recite it identically.
misconceptions.reality: While Hemacandra’s core verses are widely accepted, manuscript evidence and traditional reports indicate that one or more verses were added from other ancient texts by later ācāryas, and minor variations in wording or verse order can be found across editions and commentarial traditions. Some liturgical compilations present the stotra together with other hymns (such as Virajina Stotra and Mahādeva Stotra) as a “stotratrayī.” These variations do not alter the central theme of Sakal-arhat praise but remind readers that textual transmission is dynamic and that specific ritual uses may differ slightly between communities.
